title: Null safety — quick overview
rememberThis: int? is System.Nullable<int> at run time. string? is still System.String; the ? is an annotation.
NRT warnings are not NREs. A project can be warning-clean and still throw NullReferenceException.
Prefer ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull and real checks over !. Treat ! as a compiler lie you must own.
required forces initialization, not non-null. Combine required with a non-nullable type.
TypeScript strictNullChecks also disappears at run time. C# NRT disappears too; only Nullable<T> is a CLR type.
bullets: Enable <Nullable>enable</Nullable> (SDK templates already do). Use #nullable for mixed files.
Flow analysis tracks not-null vs maybe-null; if (x is not null) narrows x.
Auth tokens, Redis misses, and CSV cells are the usual maybe-null surfaces — annotate them, do not bang them.
Attributes (NotNullWhen, MaybeNull, NotNullIfNotNull) teach the compiler contracts it cannot infer.
Lifted operators on int? return null when an operand is null; comparisons with null are a common interview trap.

rows.label: int?
rows.value: Nullable<int>; HasValue / Value; boxing a null int? boxes to a null reference

rows.label: string?
rows.value: Same IL type as string; compiler warns on assign/dereference mismatch

rows.label: x!

rows.value: C# 11+: must be set in an initializer; can still be set to null
